tagline: Follow the South Fork uphill between two of Idaho’s scenic byways.
intro: Wildlife Canyon Scenic Byway follows the South Fork of the Payette River along Banks-Lowman Road between Idaho 55 and Idaho 21. Driving east from Banks toward Lowman, the road gains nearly a thousand feet as the river flows the other way. Visit Idaho presents this scenic byway as a route for whitewater rafting, wildlife viewing, fishing and hiking. The tourism office gives its length as 35.8 miles and its driving time as 53 minutes. The South Fork rises in the Sawtooth Wilderness and passes Grandjean and Lowman before reaching this stretch of the canyon.

Between Crouch and Lowman, road construction transformed a small unpaved road into a paved route. The improved roadway has informational and rafting pullouts and carries tourists, rafters and commuters. Garden Valley’s earlier economy rested on logging, mining and ranching; later, work as hunting guides joined those livelihoods.

Begin at Banks, where the North and South forks meet, and head east along the South Fork toward Garden Valley. Near Crouch, the Middle Fork joins the South Fork; farther east, the Deadwood River enters just west of Lowman. The drive finishes at Idaho 21 in Lowman, linking the Payette River Scenic Byway at Banks with the Ponderosa Pine Scenic Byway.

moments.title: Banks
moments.text: Two forks meet at Banks, and the names of the rafting runs change with them. The South Fork’s Staircase run ends here; the Main run begins here and follows Idaho 55 downstream toward Horseshoe Bend. Above Banks, the lower North Fork drops 1,700 feet in 16 miles through Class V rapids. Its whitewater can be viewed from Idaho 55, which closely follows the riverbank. Wildlife Canyon’s road turns toward the South Fork and Lowman. Downstream, the Main run has numerous Class III rapids, distinct from the steeper Class V water above on the North Fork.

moments.title: Crouch
moments.text: Crouch’s founding and incorporation were separate events: the town began in 1934 and incorporated in 1951 to bring legal alcohol and gambling to the area. In the surrounding Garden Valley area, logging, mining and ranching provided early livelihoods, followed by work as hunting guides. Road improvements between Crouch and Lowman changed a small unpaved road into pavement with informational and rafting pullouts. Just southwest of Crouch, the Middle Fork of the Payette joins the South Fork. That road now carries commuters as well as tourists and rafters across this part of central Idaho.

moments.title: Lowman
moments.text: Natural hot springs reach the surface in the middle of Lowman and elsewhere in the surrounding mountains. The community takes its name from Nathaniel Winfield Lowman, an Iowa homesteader who settled here in 1907. In 1989, wildfire burned more than 45,000 acres in the Lowman area and destroyed 26 structures, without injuries or deaths. A one-room school remains in use. Lowman stands on the north bank of the South Fork in central Idaho, at 3,960 feet above sea level. Here Banks-Lowman Road meets Idaho 21, the Ponderosa Pine Scenic Byway.
